title: The Ruy Lopez
subtitle: Bishop to b5 — pressure that lasts forty moves.
goals: Play the Morphy Defence move order
Prove the e5 pawn is not free in the Exchange Variation

steps.say: The Spanish Game, named for a 16th-century priest and still the most respected opening in chess. The bishop on b5 doesn't attack the king — it attacks the c6 knight, and the c6 knight is what defends the e5 pawn. This is pressure by indirection, and it can last the whole game.
Black's main reply is 3...a6, the Morphy Defence — a small move that forces a big decision. White must either retreat, keeping the tension, or take.

autoMoves.say: 3...a6, putting the question to the bishop.
4.Ba4 — the main line. The bishop keeps the pin on the a4-e8 diagonal and White plays on.
5.O-O, offering the e-pawn: the point is that after ...Nxe4 White plays d4 and regains it with a big lead in development.
6.Re1, defending e4 properly and building the classical Spanish set-up. Both sides now manoeuvre for twenty moves — that's the Ruy Lopez.

steps.say: The other choice is the Exchange Variation: 4.Bxc6 dxc6. White has given up the bishop pair to wreck Black's queenside pawns — Black now has doubled c-pawns and can never make a healthy queenside majority. In return, Black gets two bishops and open lines. You're White, and the e5 pawn looks distinctly loose.

steps.prompt: Black's e5 pawn has lost its defender. Is it really free? Decide — and play the right move.
hints: Before taking, ask what Black gets in return. Put your knight on e5 in your head and look for black moves that hit two things at once.
5.Nxe5? runs into Qd4!, forking the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 — Black wins the pawn straight back with a better position.
Castle instead. 5.O-O is the main line: safe king first, and the e5 pawn isn't going anywhere.

line.say: The correct move, and it takes discipline to play it. The e5 pawn is 'hanging' but poisoned; castling keeps every advantage of the Exchange Variation — the superior pawn structure — without handing Black activity. White's long-term plan is simply to trade everything and win the pawn endgame, where Black's doubled c-pawns cannot make a passer.

rejections.say: The trap. Black replies Qd4!, attacking your knight on e5 AND your pawn on e4 at the same time. After Nf3 Qxe4+ Black has regained the pawn with the bishop pair and an active queen — you've handed over everything the exchange on c6 won you.
Playable, but it opens the position for Black's two bishops — exactly the wrong policy when your whole advantage is a static structural one. Keep the position closed-ish and castle.
Over-protecting e4 by hand is clumsy and leaves the king in the centre. There's a move that solves king safety and keeps every structural trump.

steps.wrongSay: Count carefully before grabbing: if you put a knight on e5, is there a black move that attacks it and something else at the same time?
steps.successSay: Structural advantages are patient. The Exchange Ruy is won in the endgame, not on move five.
